analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare drug-discount and catastrophic-coverage program run through private contractors, for seniors.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2000 by 9 Republican senators, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Medicare beneficiaries voluntarily join a program that gives them a card entitling them to the discounted, negotiated drug prices of private contractors, plus a backstop covering all drug costs above a yearly limit that varies by income — $1,200 out of pocket for the poorest beneficiaries. It would waive the $35 annual fee for people under twice the poverty line, pay for the program out of Medicare's Part B trust fund, and create a new federal Medicare Prescription Drug Agency to run it. Nothing in the bill forces drug makers to cut prices directly; savings would come from whatever discounts private contractors could negotiate.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially lower-income seniors. Those below twice the poverty line pay no enrollment fee and stop paying for drugs once they hit $1,200 out of pocket in a year; those between 200% and 400% of poverty get the same protection at $2,500; wealthier beneficiaries get the discount card but no catastrophic coverage (those with income above $100,000, or $200,000 for couples, are excluded from the catastrophic benefit entirely). All enrollees get access to contractors' negotiated prices, which are typically lower than retail cash prices.

how_it_helps.text: Enrollees would get a discount card guaranteeing access to the negotiated prices contractors use to pay for prescription drugs, rather than full retail prices [S3].

A catastrophic benefit would cap annual out-of-pocket drug costs at $1,200 for beneficiaries below 200% of the poverty line, $2,500 for those between 200% and 400%, and $5,000 above that, with the federal government — not the contractor — bearing that risk [S3].
The $35 annual enrollment fee would be waived for anyone with income below 200% of the poverty line [S3].
The program would be voluntary and its costs paid from the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, with the catastrophic part funded by appropriations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Medicare Part B trust fund and direct appropriations for the catastrophic benefit and administration. Pharmaceutical makers would give up some margin on drugs sold to enrollees through the contractors' negotiated discounts — though the bill never lets Medicare itself negotiate directly with manufacturers.

drawbacks.text: The benefit depends entirely on private contractors' bids: the bill guarantees no specific discount amount, and the text explicitly has eligible entities 'compete for beneficiaries on the basis of the discounts, formularies, pharmacy networks' — so savings could be small wherever contractor competition is weak [S3].

The catastrophic thresholds are high: even the poorest beneficiaries would pay the first $1,200 out of pocket each year, and beneficiaries above 400% of poverty would pay up to $5,000, so many seniors with heavy drug costs would still face large bills [S3].

Medicare itself would never negotiate with drug manufacturers; the bill channels all purchasing through private entities like pharmacy benefit managers and insurers, and reimburses them a per-prescription administrative fee 'consistent with such fees paid under private sector pharmaceutical benefit contracts' [S3].

The bill creates a brand-new independent federal agency — the Medicare Prescription Drug Agency, with its own Senate-confirmed Commissioner, Deputy, Chief Actuary, and Inspector General — a costly and duplicative layer alongside the existing Health and Human Services bureaucracy, capped at a small staff for political appointees but still a parallel drug program to administer [S3].

High-income beneficiaries (above $100,000, or $200,000 for joint filers) are excluded from the catastrophic benefit, and the bill requires the Treasury to disclose tax-return information to the new agency to verify income — an expansion of tax-data sharing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For lower-income seniors with chronic conditions, the income-based catastrophic cap and fee waiver would have delivered real relief — for many, coverage they had nowhere else. But the design was a compromise: it bought votes for its private-sector structure by giving up the single biggest cost lever, direct Medicare negotiation with manufacturers, and it left most beneficiaries paying the first $1,200 or more of drug costs themselves. It was a genuine but partial benefit, and it still carried the open-ended federal spending of a new entitlement and a new agency.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2000, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Hagel introduced the bill on June 30, 2000, joined by seven other Republican senators as original cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind it received [S5].
The Finance Committee never acted on it, and Congress adjourned on January 3, 2001, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The pharmaceutical industry and the private drug-benefit middlemen kept the status quo: seniors continued to pay full retail prices with no Medicare drug benefit, and no negotiated-discount structure was created. Medicare beneficiaries came out with nothing. (This was also the fate of rival Democratic drug-benefit plans that year; Medicare's actual Part D drug benefit was not enacted until 2003.)

for.name: Chuck Hagel
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on June 30, 2000.

for.name: 8 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Abraham, Hutchinson, Burns, Coverdell, McCain, Ashcroft, Kyl)

against.name: William Roth
against.what_they_did: Committee chair in the 106th Congress; his committee took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All nine senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Republicans; no Democrat backed it, and it never got far enough for any vote to show a broader split.

industries.note: The bill names PBMs as eligible contractors and would have paid them an administrative fee for every prescription filled for a beneficiary, making them the permanent channel for Medicare drug benefits. Their gain came through the benefit seniors would receive, so their interest ran alongside beneficiaries' — though as private gatekeepers of formularies and discounts, they would have captured a slice of the public spending.
Pharmacy delivery systems are listed as eligible contractors and would have competed for Medicare enrollees under contracts, gaining a large new customer base financed by federal money.

Insurers and Medicare+Choice organizations could bid for contracts to provide the benefit, adding a new federally funded revenue stream. Beneficiaries would still have had to rely on them for coverage.

Contractors would negotiate discounted prices on drugs sold to enrollees, trimming manufacturers' margins on those sales — but the bill pointedly avoids direct Medicare negotiation with drug makers, leaving discounts to whatever private entities could extract, which was the industry-preferred design compared with rival universal-benefit proposals that year.
